content:
Yesterday we saw what the peace offering was; the offering of shalom, the offering where God, the priest, and the worshipper all ate from the same sacrifice. We saw that peace could only come after the burnt offering and the sin offering, because the separation had to be dealt with before the feast could begin. We saw that Christ is our shalom in person, and that His cross was the peace offering on the largest possible scale, reconciling all things in heaven and on earth through the blood of His sacrifice. Today we look at the four different animals of the peace offering and what the variety of those animals is saying about the reach of the peace that Christ made.

Each tribal leader brought four types of animals for the peace offering: two oxen, five rams, five male goats, and five male lambs of the first year. Four different categories of animal. This is not variety for the sake of abundance.
In Scripture, four consistently speaks of the whole earth; the four winds, the four corners of the earth, the four directions of the compass. When Revelation 7:1 describes the angels standing at the four corners of the earth, it is describing the complete reach of God’s sovereignty over the entire world. When Ezekiel 37:9 speaks of the breath coming from the four winds to fill the dry bones with life, it is the complete, all-directional breath of God. Four is the number of the whole earth, without a corner left out.

The four types of peace offering animals declare that the peace Christ made is not limited to one nation, one culture, one era, or one type of person.

The shalom that was purchased at the cross extends to every corner of the earth. There is no direction in which the peace of Christ does not reach. There is no tribe too remote, no people too far, no generation too late. Revelation 5:9 gives us the worship of those around the throne: “You were slain, and by Your blood You ransomed people for God from every tribe and language and people and nation.” Every tribe. Every language. Every people. Every nation. Four directions. The peace offering with four types of animals was always saying: this peace is for all four corners of the earth.

Two oxen were brought as peace offerings by each leader. The ox is the animal of strength and covenant work. We saw in studying the young bull of the burnt offering that the ox pulls the plough, bears the yoke, and produces the harvest through sustained labour. In the peace offering, the ox speaks of the powerful, covenant-grounded nature of the peace that Christ established. This is not a fragile peace that might break under pressure. It is a peace established through the full strength of Christ’s covenant work a peace that holds because the one who made it is strong enough to maintain it.

Colossians 1:20 says He reconciled all things “making peace by the blood of His cross.” The word reconcile in Greek apokatallasso carries the sense of a complete and final restoration, not a temporary truce. The two oxen of the peace offering speak of the strength and completeness of this reconciliation. And the number two in the peace offering only two oxen, while the other animals came in fives speaks of the two parties that are reconciled: Jews and Gentiles. Two oxen at the altar of peace, and two estranged parties seated at one table.

The remaining peace offering animals all came in fives. Five rams, five male goats, five male lambs of the first year. We have already seen that five is the number of grace throughout Scripture. The five books of Moses. The five smooth stones of David. The five loaves that fed five thousand. Five is the number of what God provides by His undeserved favour when human resources are insufficient. And in the peace offering, the five speaks of a peace that is not earned by the offerer. It is given.

The five rams speak of the substitutionary grace of the peace. The ram is always the animal of substitution the ram in the thicket, the ram of the priestly consecration. Five rams in the peace offering say: the peace we enjoy is a substitutionary grace. Another stood in our place so that we could stand at the table. Romans 5:10 says: “For if, while we were enemies, we were reconciled to God by the death of His Son, much more, now that we are reconciled, shall we be saved by His life.” While we were enemies. The peace was not offered to friends. It was extended to enemies through the gracious substitution of the five rams.

The five male goats in the peace offering carry a striking contrast with the single goat of the sin offering. In the sin offering, the goat bore sin and carried it away one time, sufficient and final. But in the peace offering, five goats appear at the table of fellowship. The animal that once bore the sin is now an animal of celebration. This is the transformation the cross makes possible: what was the sin-bearer becomes the fellowship animal. Those who were identified with the goat the guilty, the unclean, the outside-the-camp are now brought inside to the feast. The five goats of the peace offering say: those who needed the sin offering most are now the guests of honour at the table of shalom.

And the five lambs of the first year bring the peace offering to its fullest expression. The Passover lamb is now at the table of fellowship. The lamb that was sacrificed so the firstborn would live is now the lamb at the feast of the living. Luke 22:2-30 records Christ’s words at the Last Supper: “I assign to you, as my Father assigned to me, a kingdom, that you may eat and drink at my table in my kingdom.” The peace offering lamb points to the marriage supper of the Lamb in Revelation 19:9 the ultimate peace feast, the eternal table where all the redeemed sit together in the presence of the one whose sacrifice made the meal possible. The five lambs in the peace offering are the five of grace pointing forward to the great grace of the eternal table that is coming.

The peace offering was not only about the peace that was made. It was also about the response of those who received it. The worshipper did not just watch the peace offering from a distance. He ate it. He brought it to his household.

He shared it with his family and neighbours before Yahweh. The peace offering was a public, social, communal celebration of restored relationship. And this is the calling of the new creation believer today. We have received the shalom; we have been brought to the table, given a portion of the peace offering of Christ, reconciled to God and to one another. Now we are called to live the peace offering outward. Ephesians 2:17 says Christ “came and preached peace to you who were far off and peace to those who were near.” He is still preaching. He is preaching through us. We carry the peace offering into our homes, our relationships, our communities, and the four corners of our world. The table has room. The feast is already prepared. The four types of animals in the peace offering are still declaring: the peace of Christ reaches to every corner of the earth, and the new creation believer is the one carrying that invitation to whoever has not yet come to the table.

title: Prayer
text: Yahweh, You are the Lord of peace, who gives peace at all times and in every way (2 Thessalonians 3:16). We thank You for the four types of peace offering animals that declare Your shalom has no corner it does not reach; no tribe too remote, no person too far gone, no generation outside the reach of the peace purchased at the cross. We thank You for the grace of the five that the peace was extended to enemies, that the sin-bearer became the feast animal, that the Passover lamb is now the lamb at the eternal table. We thank You that the peace offering is not a distant transaction but a meal we are invited to eat, a table we are called to sit at, and a feast we are given to carry to others. Help us today to live as peace offering people carrying the shalom of Christ into every corner of our world, extending the invitation of the feast to those who have not yet come, and living in the fullness of the restored relationship Your Son purchased for us at such great cost. In Christ’s name, amen.
